tldr: When a humanoid lifts a heavy object, the object's mass presents a trade-off: it helps regulate inertia and momentum to enhance balance, but also strains joint torques and the foot's base of support. This study rigorously formalizes that trade-off. By incorporating a whole-body dynamics-based stability region (the Balanced State Basin, or BSB) as an explicit constraint in trajectory optimization, the authors demonstrate safe, topple-free lifting and release motions in both simulations and hardware experiments.
hero_caption: Block diagram of the overall framework proposed in this study. Contact wrenches and momentum constraints are modeled from the whole-body dynamics of the robot and the object. The Balanced State Basin (BSB) is computed for prediction and evaluation, and is embedded as a threshold constraint in whole-body trajectory optimization to achieve safe lifting control.
overview:
Expectations are rapidly growing for humanoid robots to lift and transport goods in human work environments (loco-manipulation). Much like a tightrope walker holding a long pole to stay upright, an object held in a robot's hands can act as a tool to control whole-body momentum. On the other hand, if it is too heavy, it quickly pushes joint torques and foot support boundaries past their limits. Existing control studies have not rigorously quantified this dual role of object mass on balance stability through dynamic mechanics.

To address this, the authors directly formulated the object mass parameters into the whole-body dynamics and the distributed contact wrench/center of pressure (CoP) allocation model across both feet. They then derived the Balanced State Basin (BSB)—the set of center-of-mass (CoM) states from which the robot can maintain balance without taking a step. Through both theoretical and numerical analyses, they revealed the existence of two key thresholds: the "critical mass," where balancing capability reaches its peak as mass increases, and the "transition mass," where primary limiting constraints switch between torque limits and CoP boundaries.

Furthermore, by enforcing the BSB as an inequality constraint (stability threshold) in whole-body trajectory optimization, they generated trajectories for both lift-and-hold and lift-and-release tasks. Validations in simulation and on a compact humanoid robot (ROBOTIS-OP3) showed that while conventional CoP/ZMP-margin methods fail and result in falls during demanding lifting motions, the BSB constraint fully exploits the robot's physical capabilities while successfully preventing falls.
contributions: Integrated object mass parameters into whole-body dynamics and bilateral contact wrench/CoP distribution, theoretically formulating the nonlinear trade-off between momentum regulation benefits and system/contact constraints.

Defined and quantified two crucial metrics via the whole-body Balanced State Basin (BSB): the "critical mass" where balancing capability reaches its maximum, and the "transition mass" where limiting factors switch.
Established sufficient conditions for a trajectory to maintain balanced states, even across tasks involving discontinuous mass changes such as object release.

Developed a whole-body trajectory optimization framework embedding the BSB as an explicit threshold constraint, demonstrating safe lift-and-hold and lift-and-release behaviors in simulations and on a real humanoid robot.

sections.heading: Why is balancing while lifting objects so difficult for humanoids?
sections.summary: In humanoid loco-manipulation, a carried object can serve as helpful ballast to balance, but too much weight pushes joints and feet past their limits. Existing studies rely on heuristics or machine learning, without dynamically quantifying how object mass affects balance.
sections.details:
Recent years have seen accelerated development of humanoid robots designed to adapt seamlessly to human work environments. While demand for whole-body loco-manipulation—such as carrying and lifting payloads—is surging, coordinating balance maintenance and object manipulation simultaneously remains a formidable challenge.

Just as tightrope walkers rely on balancing poles or animals use their tails to regain posture, an extra mass attached to the body can become a powerful tool to regulate momentum if used properly. In robotics, however, conventional thinking has largely stayed at the intuitive level of "too heavy means falling over." Few studies have rigorously analyzed the underlying dynamics to understand how added mass contributes to balance stability and at what precise limits it breaks down.

Existing trajectory optimization, model predictive control (MPC), and reinforcement learning frameworks sometimes account for object physical parameters, but their primary focus is task execution or parameter estimation rather than explicitly quantifying the impact on the stable region itself. This paper aims to thoroughly demystify the effects of object mass on humanoid balancing capability using full-order, nonlinear dynamics.

sections.heading: Limits of walking stability criteria and the new whole-body BSB perspective
sections.summary: Walking-oriented reduced-model metrics like ZMP or the linear inverted pendulum fall short for non-periodic, large-upper-body lifting motions. This work proposes leveraging the Balanced State Basin (BSB), the boundary of CoM states that can be sustained without stepping based on whole-body dynamics.
sections.details:
2.1 Limitations of Existing Stability Indicators in Lifting Motions
Reference-point methods—such as the Zero Moment Point (ZMP: the point where the horizontal ground reaction moment is zero), Center of Pressure (CoP), and vertical projection of the Center of Mass (CoM)—have long served as standard stability criteria for bipedal walking robots. While widely adopted for their real-time computational tractability, they do not provide necessary and sufficient conditions for toppling. Lifting motions, unlike cyclic walking, feature large and dynamic upper-body movements. Reduced models like inverted pendulums that neglect arm mass and dynamics either enforce overly conservative safety margins or dangerously miss impending instabilities.

2.2 Balanced State Basin (BSB) Based on Whole-body Dynamics
To overcome this, the authors focus on the Balanced State Basin (BSB). The BSB represents the set of all CoM positions and velocities (a region in state space) from which the system can bring itself to rest and restore equilibrium while preserving designated contacts (e.g., double support), without stepping or toppling. Any state outside the BSB inevitably leads to a fall or a step under the current contacts. While the authors introduced this concept in prior work, this paper extends it to manipulation tasks involving object mass.

2.3 Specific Contributions of This Work
The core contributions of this paper are threefold: (a) formulating joint-space and centroidal momentum dynamics that incorporate object mass, (b) predicting balancing capability via the BSB to discover the "critical mass" and "transition mass," and (c) validating whole-body trajectory optimization with embedded BSB threshold constraints for lifting control in both simulation and real hardware.

sections.heading: Is object mass a friend or foe? Momentum regulation vs. physical limits
sections.summary: The authors mathematically modeled whole-body equations of motion, centroidal momentum, and double-support ground reaction wrench/moment distribution including the object mass. A heavier object offers greater momentum control, but joint torque limits and the base of support (BoS) create an unavoidable trade-off.
sections.details:
3.1 Joint-Space Dynamics and Centroidal Momentum
Consider an $n$-degree-of-freedom robot holding a rigid object with mass $m_{\text{object}}$ and inertia tensor $\boldsymbol{I}_{\text{object}}$ at its end-effectors. In generalized coordinates, the mass matrix, Coriolis, centrifugal, and gravity terms all depend linearly on the object's mass parameters. Furthermore, translational momentum $\boldsymbol{L}$ and angular momentum $\boldsymbol{H}_c$ about the CoM incorporate object-derived components, tying directly to the rate of change of external ground reaction wrenches.

3.2 Contact Wrench and Center of Pressure (CoP) Distribution
During double support (DS), allocating the ground reaction wrench across both feet is statically indeterminate. The authors introduced a six-dimensional dimensionless parameter vector $\boldsymbol{\alpha} \in [0, 1]^6$ representing the normal force distribution ratio between feet ($\alpha_1$), the magnitude and direction of tangential friction forces and moments ($\alpha_2, \alpha_3, \alpha_4$), and the single-foot CoP location ($\alpha_5, \alpha_6$). This formulation fully describes how object dynamics propagate through joint torques and momentum to reach foot contact wrenches and CoPs.

3.3 Trade-offs and Limiting Factors in Balancing
Increasing the object mass expands the range of available linear and angular momentum regulation, enhancing the ability to resist external disturbances. In practice, however, three physical constraints stand in the way:
- Joint range of motion, velocity, and torque limits: Maximum motor torque $\boldsymbol{\tau}^{\text{UB}}$ caps both the maximum object weight and achievable accelerations.
- Base of support (BoS) and unilateral contact constraints: To prevent the feet from lifting or tipping, the normal force must be positive and the CoP must remain strictly within the foot geometry.
- Friction cone constraints: Static friction bounds that prevent the feet from slipping.

These constraints battle against the momentum-regulation benefits of added mass, producing a distinct peak—a critical point—in overall balancing capability.

sections.heading: A tale of two models: 2-DoF mechanism and real humanoid
sections.summary: The authors constructed a 2-DoF reduced model for intuitive theoretical derivation alongside a 20-DoF ROBOTIS-OP3 humanoid model for validation. Analytical solutions from the reduced model reveal the existence of a "transition mass" where limiting factors shift.
sections.details:
To achieve both clear mechanical insights and practical robotic validation, this study utilizes two complementary systems.

4.1 Humanoid Robot (ROBOTIS-OP3)
The hardware platform is the ROBOTIS-OP3, featuring 20 degrees of freedom: 2 in the neck, 3 in each arm, and 6 in each leg. It has a total mass of $3.5\,\text{kg}$, a standing height of $0.51\,\text{m}$, and a foot length $fl = 0.127\,\text{m}$. Focusing on the sagittal plane (longitudinal and vertical motions), the authors treat it as a 12-DoF planar model consisting of 9 active revolute joints and 3 floating-base degrees of freedom. The object mass $m_{\text{object}}$ is attached at the hands as a point mass.

4.2 2-DoF Reduced Mechanism and Limiting Factor Analysis
A 2-DoF inverted pendulum mechanism mounted on a massless base link (foot) was introduced, matching the equivalent link masses and lengths of the humanoid. This model strips away complex multi-link coupling, allowing direct analytical study of torque limits and base of support (BoS) effects.

By equating the condition that the CoP remains within the BoS in the initial posture with the condition that the first joint torque $\tau_1$ reaches its bound $\tau^{\text{UB}}$, the boundary where dominant constraints switch—the "transition mass $m_{\text{obj,trans}}$"—is derived as:
$$m_{\text{obj,trans}} = \frac{2\tau^{\text{UB}}}{\text{BoS}_x \cdot g} - m_1 - m_2$$

This simple equation yields clear insights:
- When lighter than the transition mass ($m_{\text{object}} < m_{\text{obj,trans}}$): Torque capacity has margin to spare, and the foot boundary (BoS) is the active balance limiter.
- When equal to the transition mass ($m_{\text{object}} = m_{\text{obj,trans}}$): Torque limits and CoP boundaries activate simultaneously.
- When heavier than the transition mass ($m_{\text{object}} > m_{\text{obj,trans}}$): Torque limits are hit first, causing balancing capability to drop sharply before the full foot support area can even be utilized.

captions.P7: The system configurations used for validation. From left to right: the ROBOTIS-OP3 humanoid robot holding an object in double support, its planar sagittal model illustrating ground reaction forces and moments, and the 2-DoF reduced mechanism used for analytical investigations.

sections.heading: Computing the Balanced State Boundary (BSB)
sections.summary: Using nonlinear optimization (SQP), the algorithm finds the maximum recoverable CoM velocity in each posture while maintaining contact, constructing the BSB. It maps how the shape and volume of the BSB expand or shrink with varying object mass.
sections.details:
To construct the BSB, the authors sample initial whole-body postures and solve a nonlinear optimization problem that maximizes the allowable initial CoM velocity $\dot{r}_x(0)$ in a specified direction (here, the anterior-posterior X-axis) that can be recovered from without losing contact.

The optimization decision variables include the control vertices $\boldsymbol{v}$ of cubic B-splines representing joint trajectories, along with ground reaction distribution parameters $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$. These are discretized via direct collocation and solved using the sequential quadratic programming (SQP) solver SNOPT.

Key constraints include:
- Dynamics constraints: Full satisfaction of joint-space equations of motion and centroidal momentum equations across the entire time interval $[0, T]$.
- System and contact constraints: Joint torque and velocity limits, conditions fixing the feet to the ground without slipping or tipping, zero contact force on non-contact bodies, and static friction cones.
- Terminal conditions: Bringing the robot to a static equilibrium state at terminal time $T$, where the CoM rests within the BoS and all velocities and accelerations are zero.
- Task constraints: Bilateral arm coordination and joint limits preventing self-collisions with the held object.

The resulting boundary of maximum recoverable velocities defines the BSB. By sweeping the object mass parameter through repeated optimizations, the expansion and shrinkage of this stability basin can be comprehensively mapped.

sections.heading: BSB-constrained trajectory optimization: Lift-and-hold vs. lift-and-release
sections.summary: Lifting motions are divided into two phases—crouch-to-stand and stabilization—with the requirement that the CoM state at the standing midpoint lies within the BSB. Sufficient conditions for balance recovery are formulated for both holding and instantly releasing the object.
sections.details:
6.1 Sufficient Conditions for Enforcing Balanced States on Trajectories
Checking stability at every continuous time step during trajectory optimization is computationally prohibitive. Here, the authors proved an important property by contradiction: under constant mass and fixed contact states, if the system occupies a balanced state (inside the BSB) at any given instant, all preceding states along that trajectory are also balanced states. If the system had breached the BSB earlier, an unavoidable fall or step would have occurred, making it impossible to maintain the target contacts later.

Moreover, when discontinuous mass changes occur—such as suddenly releasing an object—the subsequent motion is guaranteed to remain stable as long as the robot's standalone CoM state at the instant of release resides within the zero-mass BSB.

6.2 Trajectory Optimization Formulation
The lifting task is divided into Phase 1 ($[0, T_1]$, moving from crouch to intermediate standing) and Phase 2 ($[T_1, T_2]$, settling to rest). Phase 1 minimizes control effort (integrated squared joint torques), while Phase 2 identifies a feasible path to static equilibrium.

At the intermediate transition time $t = T_1$, a linearized inequality constraint based on the precomputed BSB is imposed on the CoM state:
- Lift-and-Hold: $(r_x(T_1), \dot{r}_x(T_1)) \in \text{BSB}(m_{\text{object}})$
- Lift-and-Release: $(r_{\text{robot}, x}(T_1), \dot{r}_{\text{robot}, x}(T_1)) \in \text{BSB}(m_{\text{object}} = 0)$

This intermediate threshold constraint automatically synthesizes trajectories that fully push the robot's physical capabilities during the dynamic lift while guaranteeing smooth convergence to a stable rest state once upright.

sections.heading: Numerical analyses reveal critical mass and contrasting BoS vs. torque effects
sections.summary: Numerical sweeps on both the reduced model and the humanoid confirmed that allowable disturbance velocity peaks at a "critical mass." Increasing torque limits raises the maximum manipulable mass, while enlarging the foot support area expands the BSB volume across all lighter masses.
sections.details:
7.1 Analytical Results for the Reduced Mechanism
When varying the object mass $m_{\text{object}}$ from $0$ to $5.85\,\text{kg}$ in the reduced mechanism, the recoverable anterior-posterior disturbance velocity $\dot{r}_x(0)$ peaked at a specific mass before dropping abruptly. This peak is the "Critical Mass." At this point, the rate of change of centroidal momentum was also maximized, proving that the object contributed maximally to whole-body momentum regulation.

Systematic variations of torque limits $\tau^{\text{UB}}$ and the base of support $\text{BoS}$ confirmed distinct roles:
- Enlarging the $\text{BoS}$: Substantially boosts the BSB (allowable velocity) up to the critical mass, but barely alters the ultimate maximum carryable mass.
- Increasing torque limit $\tau^{\text{UB}}$: Leaves the baseline BSB size for lighter loads unchanged, but shifts both the transition mass and maximum carryable mass significantly toward heavier payloads.

7.2 Analytical Results for the ROBOTIS-OP3 Humanoid
Similar trends were verified on the humanoid model ($3.5\,\text{kg}$ body mass). With zero step length ($sl=0$, foot length $fl$), the critical mass was $1.2\,\text{kg}$ (approx. $34\%$ of robot mass). In a staggered stance ($sl=0.5fl$, $\text{BoS}=1.5fl$), the critical mass became $0.6\,\text{kg}$ ($17\%$ of robot mass).

Additionally, analyzing varying CoM heights (waist heights) demonstrated classic inverted-pendulum behavior: higher CoM postures yielded narrower BSBs and increased vulnerability to disturbances. Webots simulations confirmed that initial perturbations inside the BSB were successfully rejected, whereas perturbations outside led to falls, validating the BSB's precision.

sections.heading: Hardware tests prove it: BSB constraint succeeds where CoP margins fail
sections.summary: ROBOTIS-OP3 hardware and simulation experiments were conducted lifting a $0.6\,\text{kg}$ payload. While a baseline trajectory constrained by traditional CoP margins toppled backward upon standing, the BSB-constrained trajectory pushed the robot to its limits and achieved rock-solid balance.
sections.details:
8.1 Lift-and-Hold Experiments
Experiments were conducted on the $3.5\,\text{kg}$ ROBOTIS-OP3 lifting and holding a $0.6\,\text{kg}$ object (half its critical mass, $17\%$ of body mass) from a crouch to a stand. As a benchmark, a trajectory was generated using standard walking balance rules: keeping the CoP within a conservative foot margin ($91.34\%$ of the BoS).

The results were night and day:
- CoP-Margin Trajectory: Although the CoP stayed strictly inside the foot margin throughout the lift, the intermediate CoM state upon reaching the upright stance landed outside the BSB. As a result, no feasible solution existed in the subsequent stabilization phase under joint velocity limits, causing both the physical robot and simulation to topple backward.
- Proposed Method (BSB Constraint): The CoM state upon standing landed precisely on the frontier of $\text{BSB}(0.6\,\text{kg})$, transitioning smoothly into stabilization and settling into a steady rest posture. On the physical robot, the lift was completed cleanly with only minor heel lift.

8.2 Lift-and-Release Experiments
A lift-and-release scenario was evaluated in simulation, where the robot stands up, releases the object onto an elevated conveyor, and returns to a crouch. The instant the object is let go, the robot's standalone CoM shifts backward discontinuously. By constraining the intermediate state to the zero-mass basin $\text{BSB}(0\,\text{kg})$, the trajectory ensured that post-release states landed safely inside the recovery region, allowing the humanoid to return to its initial crouch without falling.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future work: Toward a new standard for loco-manipulation
sections.summary: This study clarified the dual role of object mass in balance through full dynamics and established BSB-based trajectory optimization. Future steps include extending the framework to 3D spaces and building precomputed offline libraries for online MPC.
sections.details:
This work represents the first systematic formulation of the balance trade-offs introduced by object mass in humanoid loco-manipulation, analyzed through the lens of whole-body dynamics and contact wrench distribution. Identifying and demonstrating the "critical mass" (which maximizes balancing capability through momentum regulation) and the "transition mass" (which demarcates torque- vs. BoS-limited regimes) offers fundamental insights for bipedal control.

The authors outline several avenues for future research:
- Reducing Computational Cost: Deriving the BSB via nonlinear optimization currently requires offline computation. Parametric formulations leveraging the linear dependence on mass parameters or precomputed BSB databases could enable real-time model predictive control (MPC).
- Extension to 3D Motions and Stepping: While this paper focused on sagittal 2D planar motions, extending the approach to full 3D loco-manipulation involving roll/yaw dynamics, as well as integrating capture-point and stepping strategies, is an important next step.
- Integration with Online Mass Estimation: Because manipulated objects often have unknown masses in real-world scenarios, combining online system identification with BSB-guided trajectory adaptation will be essential.

takeaways: Carrying a heavier object does not automatically degrade balance; up to a certain point (the critical mass), added weight enhances disturbance rejection by expanding momentum regulation capability.

Enlarging the foot support area (BoS) increases allowable disturbance velocities across lighter loads without raising the maximum carryable weight, whereas raising joint torque limits pushes out payload capacity without enlarging the low-mass stability region.

Even when conventional ZMP/CoP margins are fully satisfied, trajectories whose CoM velocity states stray outside the BSB will inevitably topple, proving the necessity of state-space stability boundaries rooted in whole-body dynamics.

In discontinuous tasks involving mass transitions—such as releasing an object—enforcing that the post-event state lies within the post-transition BSB guarantees safe, continuous whole-body recovery trajectories.
limitations: Computing the BSB and generating trajectories relies on direct collocation and nonlinear programming (SQP), which imposes heavy computational loads and currently prevents real-time, online replanning.
Analyses and validations were restricted to sagittal 2D planar motions and double-support stances, leaving full 3D loco-manipulation with lateral sway, twisting, and stepping adaptations unverified.
Minor foot tipping occurred during physical robot experiments, causing slight behavioral discrepancies against the idealized flat-contact assumption.
